title: Tutorial
text: This page is meant to be followed along with. Every diagram below is rendered by prism while this page is built — nothing here is a screenshot, and if any step stopped working the site would fail to build.

title: Tutorial
text:
Step 0 — install
pip install prism-svg
The import name is prism; the distribution is prism-svg because prism was already taken on PyPI. Check it worked:
prism archetypes
You should see ten names. If you have uv, uvx --from prism-svg prism archetypes works without installing anything.

title: Tutorial
text:
Step 1 — your first diagram
A prism spec is YAML. It needs exactly one thing: a type, naming the archetype. Here is the smallest useful diagram there is.

import prism

spec = """
type: flow
steps:
  - label: Draft
  - label: Review
  - label: Ship
"""

prism.diagram(spec)








That is the whole loop: write YAML, get SVG. You never positioned anything — prism chose the box sizes, the spacing, the arrow geometry and the colours.
Save that YAML to first.yaml and you can do the same from a terminal:
prism render first.yaml -o first.svg

title: Tutorial
section: Step 2 — give the nodes some substance
text:
Step 2 — give the nodes some substance
Every archetype in prism consumes the same node shape. Learn it once and it works in all ten. The useful fields are sublabel, icon and accent.

spec = """
type: flow
steps:
  - label: Draft
    sublabel: outline + notes
    icon: pencil
    accent: 0
  - label: Review
    sublabel: two readers
    icon: eye
    accent: 1
  - label: Ship
    sublabel: to production
    icon: rocket
    accent: 2
"""

prism.diagram(spec)








accent is an index into the theme’s colour ramp, not a colour. That indirection is the point: the theme owns the palette, so the same spec restyles cleanly. There are 1756 icons available (prism icons), all from Lucide.

title: Tutorial
text:
Step 3 — title, subtitle, caption
These live at the top level of the spec, alongside type, because they belong to the diagram rather than to any node.

spec = """
type: flow
title: Editorial process
subtitle: for long-form pieces
caption: "Source: the house style guide"
steps:
  - {label: Draft, icon: pencil, accent: 0}
  - {label: Review, icon: eye, accent: 1}
  - {label: Ship, icon: rocket, accent: 2}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)








That inline {label: Draft, icon: pencil} form is ordinary YAML — use whichever style you find more readable.

title: Tutorial
text:
Step 4 — change the direction
Most archetypes take a small number of structural options. flow takes direction.

spec = """
type: flow
direction: down
steps:
  - {label: Draft, icon: pencil, accent: 0}
  - {label: Review, icon: eye, accent: 1}
  - {label: Ship, icon: rocket, accent: 2}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)

title: Tutorial
section: Step 5 — pick the archetype by the shape of the meaning

title: Tutorial
section: Step 6 — hierarchies, the one recursive case
text:
Step 6 — hierarchies, the one recursive case
hierarchy is the only archetype whose data nests, through children. That is data recursion, not template composition — you still cannot put one archetype inside another.

spec = """
type: hierarchy
title: A book
root:
  label: Manuscript
  icon: book
  children:
    - label: Part I
      children:
        - {label: Chapter 1}
        - {label: Chapter 2}
    - label: Part II
      children:
        - {label: Chapter 3}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)

title: Tutorial
text:
Step 7 — switch the theme
Add one line. Nothing else about the spec changes.

spec = """
type: flow
theme: dark
title: Editorial process
steps:
  - {label: Draft, icon: pencil, accent: 0}
  - {label: Review, icon: eye, accent: 1}
  - {label: Ship, icon: rocket, accent: 2}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)








Four themes ship: default, dark, paper and mono. paper is the one to reach for in print — serif typography, warm surface, hairline strokes:

prism.diagram(spec.replace("theme: dark", "theme: paper"))

title: Tutorial
text:
Step 8 — nudge a single token
You rarely need a whole new theme to change one thing. tokens: overrides individual theme values by dotted path.

spec = """
type: flow
theme: paper
tokens:
  geometry.radius: 0
  geometry.gap: 44
title: Wider gaps, square corners
steps:
  - {label: Draft, icon: pencil, accent: 0}
  - {label: Review, icon: eye, accent: 1}
  - {label: Ship, icon: rocket, accent: 2}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)








A mistyped path fails loudly rather than being ignored — try geometry.radiuss and prism will tell you what it expected.

title: Tutorial
text:
Step 9 — your own theme
For a whole document set you want a theme file of your own. Scaffold one:
prism new-theme house
That writes house.yaml here, copied from the default theme and already carrying its new name. Start from whichever bundled theme is closest:
prism new-theme house --from paper      # start from the print theme
prism new-theme house -o themes/house.yaml
The file opens with a comment explaining the two rules you have to respect, so you do not have to remember them. Then point any spec at it:
type: flow
theme: ./house.yaml
steps:
  - {label: Draft}
Edit the tokens and every diagram that references the file restyles at once.
The two rules, since they surprise people: typography.family must be grotesque, serif or mono, and typography.weight values must be 400 or 700. Those are exactly the fonts and weights whose metrics prism has vendored. Anything else would mean measuring text against a font your reader does not have, and labels would overflow their boxes. prism new-theme validates the file it writes, so a bad edit fails when you next render rather than producing a quietly broken picture.

title: Tutorial

title: Tutorial
section: Step 11 — put it in your own Quarto document
text:
Step 11 — put it in your own Quarto document
Everything above is a real Quarto page. The pattern is:
```{python}
#| label: fig-process
#| fig-cap: "The editorial process"
#| echo: false
import prism
prism.diagram("figures/process.yaml")
```
prism.diagram() accepts a path or a spec string and returns an object that knows how to display itself, so Quarto embeds the SVG directly — no intermediate file and no rasterisation. See In Quarto for PDF output and batch rendering.

And when you want a field prism does not have, prism schema <archetype> is the authoritative answer on what a given archetype accepts.

title: In Quarto
text: prism was built with books in mind as much as agents. Diagrams are SVG, so they stay sharp at any size, keep their text selectable and searchable, and diff sensibly in git.

title: In Quarto
text:
The short version
prism results render themselves in any IPython-compatible environment, which includes Quarto’s Jupyter engine. Return the object from a code cell:
```{python}
#| label: fig-pipeline
#| fig-cap: "The ingestion pipeline"
#| echo: false
import prism
prism.diagram("pipeline.yaml")
```
prism.diagram() returns an object with a _repr_svg_, so Quarto embeds the SVG inline — no intermediate file, no rasterisation.

title: In Quarto
In Quarto
In Quarto
text:
Rendering to PDF
Quarto’s Typst and LaTeX paths both accept SVG figures. Because prism paints its own surface colour, a figure keeps its intended background rather than inheriting the page.
One caveat worth stating plainly: prism measures text against the metrics of Arial, Times New Roman and Courier New. Those have metric-compatible clones almost everywhere (Helvetica on macOS; Liberation or Croscore on Linux), so boxes fit. If you override typography.family with a font prism has not measured, expect looser boxes — see Themes.

title: In Quarto
text:
Batch rendering
For a manuscript with many figures, render them all ahead of the build:
for spec in figures/*.yaml; do
  prism render "$spec" -o "figures/$(basename "${spec%.yaml}").svg"
done
The same approach builds this site’s gallery — see scripts/build_gallery.py in the repository, which renders every bundled example in every bundled theme and generates the Catalog and Themes pages from the result. Documentation that is generated from the examples cannot drift from them.

title: Catalog
text:
prism ships 10 archetypes. Each one is opinionated: you describe the meaning of the picture and prism decides the geometry, spacing and colour.
Every diagram below is generated from the YAML shown beside it, by the same code path the library exposes. If an example stopped rendering, this page could not be built.

For agents
text:
prism is built to be driven by a language model. The agent does the part models are good at — reading prose and deciding what shape the idea has — and prism does the part models are bad at: geometry, spacing, alignment and colour.
prism itself never calls a model. It is deterministic: the same spec always produces byte-identical SVG.

title: For agents
text:
The envelope
Every spec is a YAML mapping whose top-level type selects an archetype.
type: flow                   # required — one of the ten archetypes
theme: default               # bundled name, or a path to your own YAML
title: "Ingestion pipeline"  # optional
subtitle: "as of Q3"         # optional
caption: "Source: review"    # optional
width: 900                   # layout hint in px; height follows the content
tokens:                      # optional per-spec theme overrides, dotted paths
  palette.ink: "#0b1020"
Everything else in the mapping is the archetype’s own payload.

title: For agents
text:
The shared node
Every archetype consumes the same node shape. This is the vocabulary worth memorising, because it is the same in all ten:
id: ingest                 # optional; needed only when something references it
label: "Ingest"            # required
sublabel: "S3 + Kafka"     # optional
icon: database             # optional; a Lucide icon name
badge: "1"                 # optional; at most 4 characters
accent: 2                  # optional; ramp index 0-5, or a palette token name
emphasis: normal           # strong | normal | muted
note: "runs nightly"       # optional; `flow` and `timeline` only
A badge is a short marker — a step number, a version, a count — drawn as a filled pill inside the top-right of the node. Four characters is the cap, so it never wraps. Every archetype that draws a node box draws its badge.
A note is a marginal annotation: muted, small, and set outside the node, below it in a left-to-right layout and beside it in a top-down one. Only flow and timeline have a free margin to put one in; on the other eight archetypes a note raises an error rather than being silently dropped, so an agent that emits one gets told instead of shipping a picture that quietly lost it. Fold the text into sublabel there.

title: For agents
text:
Getting the schema
prism schema flow
emits JSON Schema for the archetype’s payload, suitable for structured output or a tool definition. Every archetype rejects unknown fields, so a typo fails loudly at validation rather than silently rendering the wrong picture.

title: For agents
text:
Icons
prism vendors all 1756 Lucide icons. That is far too many for a model to choose from reliably, so use this shortlist and reach for prism icons only when nothing here fits:
activity triangle-alert archive bell book box brain briefcase building calendar chart-line check circle-check clock cloud code cog compass cpu credit-card database eye file-text funnel flag flask-conical folder gauge git-branch globe hammer heart key-round layers lightbulb link lock mail map-pin message-circle package pencil phone chart-pie play plug rocket search send server settings shield shield-check shopping-cart sparkles sprout star target terminal trending-up truck upload users wallet wrench zap
An unknown icon name fails with a suggestion rather than rendering a blank.

title: For agents
section: Errors are part of the interface
text:
Errors are part of the interface
prism’s exceptions are written for a recovery loop, not for a stack trace. Each one names the offending value and points at the valid neighbours:
unknown icon 'databse' — did you mean: database, data-flow?
unknown archetype 'flowchart' — did you mean: flow?
unknown token 'palette.inc' — did you mean: palette.ink, palette.line?
cell references unknown row 'emae'; known rows: ['emea', 'amer', 'apac']
era 'Pre-revenue' spans unknown event id(s) ['sed']; known ids: ['seed', 'beta']
An agent’s ability to fix its own output is bounded by the quality of the error string, so this is treated as a feature surface rather than as diagnostics.

title: For agents
text:
Choosing an archetype
The decision is about the shape of the meaning, not the subject matter:



If the content is…
Use




ordered steps, a process, a pipeline
flow


containment or reporting structure
hierarchy


a process that returns to its start
cycle


events in time
timeline


two or more options weighed against each other
comparison


items placed against two independent dimensions
quadrant


layers of magnitude, or stages that shed volume
pyramid


tiers of a system, bottom to top
stack


one centre with several dependents
hub


values at the intersection of two lists
matrix



When two fit, prefer the one with fewer nodes on screen.

title: prism
text: prism turns a short YAML spec into a single, well-designed SVG diagram. You describe what the picture means; prism decides the geometry, spacing, typography and colour.

title: prism
text:
Why this exists
Diagram-as-code tools — Mermaid, PlantUML, D2, Graphviz — model graph topology. They are very good at that. But a great many explanatory pictures are not graphs: pyramids, funnels, quadrants, timelines, comparisons, radial hubs. Those tools have no vocabulary for them, and theming is an afterthought, so the output reads as an engineering diagram rather than an explainer.
At the other end, tools like Napkin AI have exactly that vocabulary but ship it as closed SaaS with no library surface.
prism is the missing middle: an open, template-rich, themeable, agent-first library that takes a declarative spec and renders a designed picture.

title: prism
text:
Design in three sentences
One spec, one diagram. No multi-diagram documents, no charts, no prose-to-diagram — prism never calls a language model. An agent (or a person) writes the spec; prism deterministically renders it.
Deep templates, no nesting. Complexity lives inside an archetype — rich typed nodes, swimlanes, era bands, axes — plus one generic groups: construct. Recursive schemas are where small models fail, and good-looking nesting needs per-combination tuning that never converges.
Themes are data. A theme is a token set in YAML. Archetypes read tokens only; a literal colour inside an archetype is a bug.

title: prism
text:
Install
pip install prism-svg      # import name is `prism`
Its only runtime dependencies are tesserax (pure-Python SVG and layout), PyYAML and pydantic.

title: prism
text:
Use it
import prism

prism.render("pipeline.yaml", "pipeline.svg")
svg = prism.render_str(spec_text)          # returns the SVG as a string
prism render spec.yaml -o out.svg
prism archetypes                # list the catalog
prism themes                    # list bundled themes
prism icons                     # list available icon names
prism schema flow               # JSON Schema, for tool calling
In a notebook or a Quarto document, the result renders inline — see In Quarto.

title: prism
text:
What’s here

Catalog — all ten archetypes, each with the spec that produced it.
Themes — the four bundled themes, and how to write your own.
For agents — the closed vocabulary, JSON Schema, and error design.

title: prism
text:
One detail worth knowing
Every label in a prism diagram is measured against vendored font metrics before its box is drawn. That sounds like a footnote; it is the difference between a diagram and a mess. The usual shortcut — estimating text width as characters x size x 0.6 — is wrong by +116% on lllll and −28% on MMMMM, so boxes come out either absurdly padded or overflowing their borders.
prism vendors advance-width tables for the three font stacks that have metric-compatible clones on every platform (Arial, Times New Roman, Courier New), wraps text itself, and hands true bounds to the layout engine. That is also why typography.family and typography.weight are restricted: prism only offers what it can measure.

title: Themes
text:
A theme is data, not code — a token set in YAML covering palette, typography and geometry. Archetypes read tokens only; a literal colour anywhere in an archetype is a bug.
Because the tokens are semantic (ink, surface, muted) rather than literal (black, white), dark mode falls out for free.
Any spec can also override individual tokens inline by dotted path:
Or point theme: at your own YAML file, which is how you brand a whole document set.

title: Themes
text:
Writing your own
Scaffold a theme file from whichever bundled theme is closest:
prism new-theme house                 # from `default`
prism new-theme house --from paper    # from the print theme
prism new-theme house -o themes/house.yaml
Then point a spec at it with theme: ./house.yaml. The generated file carries a header explaining the two constraints, which are enforced at load time:

typography.family must be grotesque, serif or mono — the three stacks whose font metrics prism vendors.
typography.weight.* must be 400 or 700, for the same reason. A weight prism has not measured would be synthesised by the viewer at a width prism never accounted for, and labels would overflow their boxes.
